question: How does volume behave when symmetric convex shapes are interpolated?
idea: The manuscript claims the logarithmic Brunn–Minkowski inequality, which controls volume under a specified interpolation of origin-symmetric convex bodies. It also gives concavity results for scaling under even log-concave measures. Symmetry and convexity are essential; the statement does not describe arbitrary shapes or arbitrary probability distributions.
why: The study of shapes and distances. Convex shapes have no inward dents; metric geometry asks what can be learned from distances alone.

glossary.meaning: A shape is convex if the straight segment between any two of its points stays inside the shape.
A mathematical statement proposed to be true but requiring proof or a counterexample.
A way of measuring the number of independent directions or degrees of freedom; different theories use different notions.

exactClaim: Proves the logarithmic Brunn–Minkowski inequality for origin-symmetric convex bodies in every dimension, and the scalar-dilation B-conjecture for all even log-concave Radon measures. For Lebesgue volume it also proves the additive Lp Brunn–Minkowski inequality for full-dimensional origin-symmetric convex bodies throughout $0\lt p\lt 1$. )
